These exercises practise the ideas from Chapter 6: sampling distributions, confidence intervals, t-tests, effect sizes, and chi-square tests. Several of the answers are *not* significant. That is part of the lesson: a non-significant result is still a result. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.


::: {.cell setup='true' exercise='["ex1","ex2","ex3","ex4","ex5","ex6"]'}
```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5, ex6]
library(dplyr)
students  <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
first_sem <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 1) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id))
```
:::


## Sampling and confidence

### Exercise 1: Two sampling distributions

Draw 1,000 samples of 10 students' first-semester study hours, and 1,000 samples of 50. Compare the spread (SD) of the two sets of averages. Which is smaller, and why?


::: {.cell exercise='ex1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
study <- first_sem$study_hours[!is.na(first_sem$study_hours)]
set.seed(1)
means_10 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(study, 10)))
means_50 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(study, ______)))
sd(means_10)
sd(______)
hist(means_50)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
study <- first_sem$study_hours[!is.na(first_sem$study_hours)]
set.seed(1)
means_10 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(study, 10)))
means_50 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(study, 50)))
sd(means_10)
sd(means_50)
hist(means_50)
```

The averages of 50 students vary much less (an SD of about 1.8 hours, against about 4.2 for samples of 10). Larger samples give more precise estimates: the standard error shrinks with $\sqrt{n}$.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: A confidence interval

Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the average first-semester GPA.


::: {.cell exercise='ex2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
t.test(first_sem$______)$conf.int
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
t.test(first_sem$gpa)$conf.int
```

The average GPA of graduate students is plausibly between about 3.08 and 3.13. The interval is narrow because 600 students give a precise estimate.
:::
:::

## t-tests

### Exercise 3: Is wellbeing different from 60?

Test whether the average first-semester wellbeing is different from 60. What do you conclude?


::: {.cell exercise='ex3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
t.test(first_sem$wellbeing, mu = ______)
```
:::


::: { .hint exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

$H_0$: the average is 60. Look at the p-value and at whether the confidence interval includes 60.
:::
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
t.test(first_sem$wellbeing, mu = 60)
```

The average is 60.5, the confidence interval (about 59.5 to 61.4) includes 60, and the p-value is about 0.35. There is no evidence that average wellbeing differs from 60. That does not prove it is exactly 60: only that the data is consistent with it.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: Full-time against part-time

Do full-time and part-time students differ in first-semester GPA? Run a two-sample t-test, then calculate Cohen's *d*.


::: {.cell exercise='ex4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
t.test(gpa ~ ______, data = first_sem)

full <- first_sem$gpa[first_sem$study_mode == "Full-time"]
part <- first_sem$gpa[first_sem$study_mode == "Part-time"]
(mean(full) - mean(part)) / sqrt((var(full) + var(______)) / 2)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
t.test(gpa ~ study_mode, data = first_sem)

full <- first_sem$gpa[first_sem$study_mode == "Full-time"]
part <- first_sem$gpa[first_sem$study_mode == "Part-time"]
(mean(full) - mean(part)) / sqrt((var(full) + var(part)) / 2)
```

Both groups average about 3.10, the p-value is about 0.9, and Cohen's *d* is almost exactly 0. Part-time students have lower *wellbeing* (Chapter 4), but not lower grades.
:::
:::

## Categorical data

### Exercise 5: Living away and dropout

Is living away from family related to considering dropout? Make the table, look at the proportions, and run a chi-square test.


::: {.cell exercise='ex5'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
away <- table(students$lives_away, students$______)
away
prop.table(away, margin = 1)
chisq.test(away)
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
away <- table(students$lives_away, students$considering_dropout)
away
prop.table(away, margin = 1)
chisq.test(away)
```

17% of students who live away from family have considered dropping out, against 14% of those who do not, but the p-value is about 0.31: a difference this size could easily be chance. (For a 2 × 2 table, R applies a small correction, named in the output as Yates' continuity correction.)
:::
:::

### Exercise 6: Check the expected counts

Is the chi-square test from Exercise 5 reliable? Check that every expected count is at least 5.


::: {.cell exercise='ex6'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex6
away <- table(students$lives_away, students$considering_dropout)
chisq.test(away)$______
```
:::


::: { .solution exercise="ex6" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
away <- table(students$lives_away, students$considering_dropout)
chisq.test(away)$expected
```

The smallest expected count is about 38, far above 5, so the test is reliable.
:::
:::
